Q: Handle all HTTPS redirects in top level .htaccess, when subdir .htaccess exists. .htaccess nesting problem A:

In your www/api/.htaccess use RewriteOptions InheritBefore on top of your .htaccess:

RewriteOptions InheritBefore
RewriteEngine On
RewriteRule ^flight/ flight.php [L]

As per official (linked) doc:

InheritBefore
This forces the current configuration to inherit the configuration of the parent, but the rules from the parent scope are applied before rules specified in the child scope. Available in Apache HTTP Server 2.3.10 and later.

Q: MS Access VBA, Call Function, but goto a specific line of function A:

You can open the Form in dialog mode. This pauses the code at DoCmd.OpenForm. When you close the Form, the code resumes after DoCmd.OpenForm.

DoCmd.OpenForm "Form1", WindowMode:=acDialog

Alternatively, if you want to keep the Form open, you can hide the form without closing it, call DoEvents and then display it again. This will resume the code as well.

In a button click:

Private Sub Command0_Click()
    Me.Visible = False
    DoEvents
    Me.Visible = True
End Sub

Yet another possibility is to extract the rest of this program into a Sub in a Module. Then you can call it from both, the function CopyDSTM and from the button click in your Form.

Q: extracting particular numbers from a column of characters based on a criterion A:

We can use strcapture for this:

strcapture("([0-9]+) *: *([0-9]+)", col[[1]], list(year=0L, month=0L)) |>
  na.omit()
#     year month
# 8   1996     1
# 21  1997     1
# 34  1998     1
# 47  1999     1
# 60  2000     1
# 73  2001     1
# 86  2002     1
# 99  2003     1
# 112 2004     1
# 125 2005     1
# 138 2006     1
# 151 2007     1
# 164 2008     1
# 177 2009     1
# 190 2010     1
# 203 2011     1
# 216 2012     1
# 229 2013     1
# 242 2014     1
# 255 2015     1
# 268 2016     1
# 281 2017     1
# 294 2018     1
# 307 2019     1
# 320 2020     1
# 333 2021     1
# 346 2022     1
# 359 2023     1
# 372 2024     1
# 385 2025     1
# 398 2026     1

Since you want to keep the non-year months as well, then

library(dplyr)
col |>
  filter(grepl("[0-9]", `...1`)) |>
  mutate(
    y = if_else(grepl(":", `...1`), trimws(sub(":.*", "", `...1`)), NA),
    m = trimws(if_else(grepl(":", `...1`), sub(".*:", "", `...1`), `...1`))
  )
# # A tibble: 361 × 3
#    ...1      y     m    
#    <chr>     <chr> <chr>
#  1 1996 :  1 1996  1    
#  2 2         <NA>  2    
#  3 3         <NA>  3    
#  4 4         <NA>  4    
#  5 5         <NA>  5    
#  6 6         <NA>  6    
#  7 7         <NA>  7    
#  8 8         <NA>  8    
#  9 9         <NA>  9    
# 10 10        <NA>  10   
# # ℹ 351 more rows
# # ℹ Use `print(n = ...)` to see more rows

And if you want to include a portion from a previous question, then add |> fill(year) to the end :-)

(I used dplyr in that second code block, but it can easily be done in base R if desired.)

For the "last", we can add some more code,

dat <- col |>
  filter(grepl("[0-9]", `...1`)) |>
  mutate(
    y = if_else(grepl(":", `...1`), trimws(sub(":.*", "", `...1`)), NA),
    m = trimws(if_else(grepl(":", `...1`), sub(".*:", "", `...1`), `...1`)),
    across(c(y, m), ~ as.integer(.x))
  ) |>
  fill(y)

The last year and last year/month:

slice_max(dat, order_by = data.frame(y, m))
# # A tibble: 1 × 3
#   ...1          y     m
#   <chr>     <int> <int>
# 1 2026 :  1  2026     1

If you want the last month of each year,

slice_max(dat, by = y, order_by = m)
# # A tibble: 31 × 3
#    ...1      y     m
#    <chr> <int> <int>
#  1 12     1996    12
#  2 12     1997    12
#  3 12     1998    12
#  4 12     1999    12
#  5 12     2000    12
#  6 12     2001    12
#  7 12     2002    12
#  8 12     2003    12
#  9 12     2004    12
# 10 12     2005    12
# # ℹ 21 more rows
# # ℹ Use `print(n = ...)` to see more rows

Q: How to get the local time zone name in Rust? A:

To the best of my understanding, determining the timezone name is not possible with chrono{-tz}. There seems to be an issue titled Detecting system timezone, but it lacks all details.

Update: New crate found, which actually gives the more precise desired result.

The best crate I have found is iana-time-zone, which has only one single function to determine the name of the local timezone like so:

let tz_name = iana_time_zone::get_timezone()
    .expect("Could not determine timezone.");
println!("Timezone name: {tz_name}");

Running the code gives the following output:

Timezone name: America/Denver

Briefly looking at the source code, it appears th crate has a wide platform support with implementations for target_os of aix, android, dragonfly, freebsd, haiku, hurd, illumos, ios, linux, macos, netbsd, openbsd, solaris, wasm32 and windows.

On Debian and illumos, the string appears to always represent the exact timezone set. However on FreeBSD I consistently get Europe/Berlin even if Europe/Copenhagen or Europe/Oslo has been configured. That's unexpected but not a problem, since they are all the same.


Older answer below: Highly unlikely to be of interest.

With the tz-rs crate though, one can use the following code:

let tz = tz::TimeZone::local()
    .expect("Unable to determine timezone");
let tz_name = tz
    .find_current_local_time_type()
    .expect("Could not find local timezone type")
    .time_zone_designation();
println!("Timezone name: {tz_name}");

Running the above, with my timezone set to America/Denver, results in the following output:

Timezone name: MST

Which is at least is an abbreviation.
